summary:
A press release covering Monster's Beauty Bias at Work Report, published via Allwork.Space (dated August 31, 2026, Guaynabo, P.R.). The survey of 1,003 US workers examines perceptions of appearance-based bias in hiring, promotion and day-to-day workplace treatment.

Headline finding: 88% of workers believe conventionally attractive people have an advantage in hiring and promotions, split between 43% who call it a major advantage and 45% a slight advantage; only 12% see no real advantage.

Appearance concerns also suppress job seeking: 32% said they have avoided applying for a job entirely due to concerns about their appearance. Nearly half (47%) reported at least one negative career or workplace experience tied to appearance, including 24% treated less professionally or taken less seriously, 16% who believe appearance contributed to not being hired, 15% passed over for a promotion or other opportunity, 14% who felt pressured to change their appearance to fit workplace expectations, and 8% who received negative feedback about their looks.

On conformity pressure, 62% have felt pressure to meet a workplace appearance standard (37% mild, 25% strong), while 38% have not. One third (33%) receive feedback prompting appearance change frequently (9%) or occasionally (24%), versus 27% rarely and 40% never.

Gender gap: 70% believe women face more appearance pressure (41% significantly more, 29% somewhat more), 7% say men face more, and 23% say pressure is about equal.

Vicki Salemi, Monster Career Expert, said workers want opportunities based on skills and experience, but the findings show appearance can feel like an added factor to navigate, becoming a workplace issue when people are judged before demonstrating capability.

Methodology covered perceptions and experiences around appearance standards, self-presentation, video and social media pressure, and appearance-related spending. Sample: 53% female, 47% male, spread across age bands from 18-24 to 65-plus.
